verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that this Meccan sūrah promises persecuted believers that God will favor them, make them leaders and heirs, establish them in power, and make their oppressors see what they fear. It presents part of Moses’ story as the pattern for this promise: Pharaoh oppressed the Children of Israel and killed their sons, yet God caused Moses to be raised in Pharaoh’s own household, brought him out to Midian, returned him with manifest authority, drowned Pharaoh and his army, made the Children of Israel heirs, and gave Moses the Torah as guidance. The believers’ destiny is accordingly promised to be one of dominance, honor, integrity, and authority, and the Prophet is promised an ultimately successful return.

The sūrah then establishes the wisdom of a divinely revealed book calling to truth, answers the unbelievers’ demand, “Why is he not given the like of what was given to Moses? (28:48),” and their excuse, “If we follow the guidance with you, we shall be carried off from our country.” It concludes with a warning through Korah’s humiliating swallowing up. The context identifies the sūrah as Meccan, and the present section concerns Moses from his birth until his maturity. Regarding “Ṭāʾ sīn mīm” and the clear Book, the commentary refers to its previous explanations of similar verses.

On (28:3), Al-Mizan holds that God recites only a portion of the account of Moses and Pharaoh, “with truth,” either because the act of recital is a true divine revelation untouched by devils or because the account itself is enveloped in truth and hence beyond doubt. It is recited for the benefit of those who believe in God’s signs: the oppressed followers of the Prophet are to reflect on how God raised Moses amid seemingly hopeless conditions, saved and strengthened the humiliated Children of Israel, and destroyed Pharaoh’s power. The narrative therefore assures the Prophet and his believers that God will deal with the Quraysh’s tyrants as He dealt with Pharaoh and will make the oppressed believers leaders and heirs.

On (28:4), Pharaoh’s “exaltation” means the arrogant display of power. “The land” is Egypt, and his making its people shiyaʿan means dividing them into parties so that they could not unite or resist him, a means by which rulers enlarge and entrench their authority. The weakened party was the Children of Israel, descendants of Jacob who had long settled in Egypt. Pharaoh treated them as captive slaves and sought to eliminate their men by slaughtering their sons while sparing their daughters. Such unequal domination and the deprivation of one group for another’s undeserved advantage are corruption that leads humanity to destruction. The verse thus depicts the destructive conditions surrounding Moses’ birth and aimed at his annihilation.

On (28:5-6), Al-Mizan says that God’s manna is a weighty and significant favor, here bestowed by action rather than by the reproachful verbal claiming of a favor. The more apparent reading makes God’s continuing intent to favor the oppressed a circumstantial clause: while Pharaoh persecuted them, God intended to favor them. He would make them Imams—leaders and exemplars who would be followed after having been followers—make them inherit land formerly possessed by others, and establish them in a land they could own and settle after having possessed no secure abode. He would also make Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their hosts witness the very outcome they feared: that the Children of Israel would overcome them and take their kingdom, wealth, and way of life. Beneath Pharaoh’s apparently complete domination and his campaign to extinguish every possible source of resistance lay God’s irrevocable decision to rescue the Children of Israel and transfer the advantages of Pharaoh’s powerful people to those who had been oppressed.

On 28:7, al-īḥāʾ is a secret communication, including God’s inspired instruction cast into a creature’s heart and, in another usage, His communication with prophets and messengers; al-ilqāʾ means casting, and al-yamm denotes a sea or large river. The verse presupposes Moses’ conception and birth amid these severe conditions. God inspired his mother to nurse him while safe, but, if she feared Pharaoh’s people would discover and kill him, to cast him into the river—identified as the Nile in a transmitted tradition—without fear for his possible death or grief at separation. God would return him to her and make him a messenger to Pharaoh’s people and the Children of Israel. His promised return grounds the command not to grieve. In this context, fear concerns a possible misfortune, whereas grief concerns one regarded as certain.

On (28:8), al-iltiqāṭ means unexpectedly finding and picking up something, and Moses being called ḥazanan means that he would become the cause of Pharaoh’s family’s grief. Their taking him up had the eventual consequence that he would become their enemy and cause of grief. Al-Mizan distinguishes al-khāṭiʾ from one who intends an act correctly but encounters an unintended contrary outcome: Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their hosts were “erroneous” because, while violently trying to avert the loss of their kingdom, they killed Israelite boys yet preserved and carefully raised the very one through whom their kingdom would perish. Thus the term does not here mean merely that they were sinful and consequently punished by being made to raise their enemy.

On (28:9), Pharaoh’s wife interceded for Moses when he was brought from the river. “A refreshment of the eye” means that he was the delight of both their eyes, and her plural command not to kill him indicates the several persons involved in a killing: its instigator, supervisor, commander, and executor. God had cast love for Moses into her heart, so she sought to prevent his murder and clasped him to herself, as expressed in: And I cast down upon you love from Me, and that you might be brought up before My eyes. Her hope that he would benefit them or be adopted arose from the signs of greatness and divine charisma she saw in him; adoption also indicates that she and Pharaoh had no son. They did not perceive the reality or ultimate consequence of what they were doing.

On (28:10), Moses’ mother’s heart being “free” means free of fear and grief, not emptied of reason, inspiration, or all thought except Moses. Freedom from anxiety prevented the confused and disturbing thoughts that would have led her to disclose his existence. God’s inspiration—“And do not fear nor grieve; We will bring him back to you and make him one of the messengers (28:7)”—fortified her heart. She was certainly close to exposing Moses’ birth had God not strengthened her, so that she could trust His protection, be patient, cease worrying, and preserve the secret. The context rejects the cited alternative interpretations, as well as the view that the response to law-lā is omitted; the grammatical issue has been addressed in the commentary on (12:24).

On (28:11), al-qaṣṣ means tracking someone’s traces unobtrusively, from which al-qaṣaṣ, a narrative whose successive elements follow one another, is derived. Moses’ mother instructed his sister to follow him and discover what became of him. She watched from afar as Pharaoh’s servants picked him up, without their realizing that she was observing him.

On (28:12), God’s preventing Moses from accepting other foster mothers was a creational decree, not a legal prohibition: He made Moses refuse every wet-nurse before his sister approached Pharaoh’s people. The context implies that, after he repeatedly refused their nurses, his sister offered to show them a household that would care for him faithfully; she was thereby able to direct them to his own mother.

On (28:13), the narrative implies that Pharaoh’s people accepted the sister’s proposal and turned Moses over to his mother. God returned him to refresh her eye, remove her grief, and give her witnessed certainty of His promise’s truth. She had already believed the promise, but direct fulfillment gave certainty by sight. “The promise of Allah” is not confined to the particular promise of Moses’ return and messengership; rather, it is God’s unrestricted promise, true without exception. Most people lack such certainty and inward trust in God’s promises.

On (28:14), maturity is the stage at which human strength and faculties intensify, generally considered to occur at eighteen. Istawā denotes straightness, stability, firmness, and the settled condition of a person’s life, which normally follows maturity though its timing differs among people. At this point God granted Moses wisdom and knowledge, in accordance with His reward for those who do good.

verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that God recites to the Prophet only a portion of the account of Moses and Pharaoh, “with truth.” This may mean that the divine act of recital is a true revelation, free of satanic interference, or that the account itself is enveloped in truth and therefore admits no doubt. It is recited for the benefit of those who believe in God’s signs.

The intended believers are the Prophet’s persecuted and humbled followers. By reflecting on the story, they may know with certainty that the God in whom they believe is the One who raised Moses under Pharaoh’s all-encompassing tyranny, revived the truth, saved the Children of Israel from their humiliation, and strengthened them after Pharaoh had slaughtered their sons and spared their daughters. God raised Moses in his enemy’s household, brought him out of Egypt, returned him with authority, rescued the Children of Israel through him, and destroyed Pharaoh and his army.

Thus the account assures the Prophet and his believers that God will deal with the Quraysh’s tyrants as He dealt with Pharaoh and will favor Mecca’s oppressed believers by making them leaders and heirs, as He did the Children of Israel.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh’s exaltation in “the land,” meaning Egypt, was an arrogant display of power and domination. His making the people shiyaʿan means dividing them into parties so that they could neither unite upon a common position nor resist him; rulers employ such division to extend and entrench their authority. His sparing their women means letting them live.

The party he weakened was the Children of Israel, descendants of Jacob who had settled and multiplied in Egypt. Pharaoh treated them as captive slaves and intensified their persecution until he ordered the killing of their sons while sparing their daughters, intending thereby to eradicate their men and wipe out their community.

The commentary calls this mischief because creation does not discriminate among human groups in their basic standing; it directs them to a social life in which each receives according to worth and social cooperation. Making one group free and another enslaved, granting one what it does not deserve, and withholding from another what it does deserve are corruption leading humanity to destruction. The verse thus describes the conditions of Moses’ birth, when destructive forces encompassed the Children of Israel and sought to annihilate Moses.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that al-mann originally denotes something weighty, and al-minna is therefore a significant favor. It may be bestowed by action, as in God’s favoring the oppressed here, or claimed verbally; the latter is blameworthy except in response to manifest ingratitude. To grant them power in the land means to give them a land and abode that they possess and in which they settle.

The more apparent reading takes “While We desired to bestow a favor” as describing the condition of the party Pharaoh oppressed: while he persecuted them, God continuously intended to favor them. The successive clauses describe that favor. God would make the oppressed Imams, leaders and exemplars followed after they had themselves been followers; make them heirs of land once possessed by others; and establish them in a secure abode of their own after they had possessed none except by others’ permission.

God would also show Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their hosts what they feared from the persecuted Children of Israel: their overcoming them and taking their kingdom, wealth, and manner of life. Thus, beneath Pharaoh’s apparent total power, terror, and campaign to destroy every Israelite male and every prospect of revolt lay God’s decision to rescue them and transfer the advantages held by Pharaoh’s powerful people to those who were humble and oppressed. God decides, and nothing rescinds His decision.

Al-Mizan explains that al-īḥāʾ is a secret divine communication, including inspiration or an instruction cast into the heart; it can also describe God’s communication with prophets and messengers. Al-ilqāʾ means casting, and al-yamm is a sea or large river. The verse concisely presupposes Moses’ conception and birth amid severe hardship, after which God inspired his mother.

She was to nurse him while she did not fear Pharaoh’s people would discover and kill him; if she feared this, she was to cast him into the river—identified as the Nile in a transmitted tradition. She was not to fear his possible death or grieve at losing and being separated from him, for God would return him to her and make him a messenger to Pharaoh’s people and the Children of Israel. The promise of return justifies the command not to grieve. Here al-khawf concerns an unfortunate event that may occur, whereas al-ḥuzn concerns one regarded as certain.

Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their hosts were “erroneous” because, trying through violence to prevent the loss of their kingdom and authority, they unlawfully killed many Israelite boys but preserved and carefully raised Moses, the very one through whom their kingdom would perish. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the interpretation that calls them merely sinful people whom God punished by making them raise their own enemy; the verse instead stresses the error of their futile attempt to alter destiny.

Al-Mizan explains that Moses’ mother’s heart being “free” means that it was free of fear and grief, rather than emptied of reason, divine inspiration, or all thoughts except Moses. Such freedom prevented the confused anxiety that would have caused her to disclose the secret of her son’s birth.

God strengthened and fortified her heart through His inspiration: And do not fear nor grieve; We will bring him back to you and make him one of the messengers (28:7). She was certainly close to revealing Moses’ existence had God not given her this strength. Her being among the believers means being assured of God’s protection, patiently abandoning anxiety, and keeping Moses’ matter hidden.

The commentary rejects the cited alternative readings because the context does not support them, including the claim that she lost her mind, forgot the inspiration, or thought only of Moses. It likewise rejects the view that the response to law-lā is omitted; the relevant grammatical discussion has already appeared in the commentary on (12:24).

Moses’ mother told his sister to track him and discover what became of him. The sister watched from afar as Pharaoh’s servants picked him up, without their realizing that she was observing him.

The context implies that, after he repeatedly refused their nurses, his sister saw the situation and offered to show them a household that would care for him faithfully. In this way, she was able to direct them to Moses’ own mother.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse implies an omitted stage in the narrative: Moses’ sister offered to lead Pharaoh’s people to a suitable household, they accepted, and she led them to Moses’ mother, to whom they returned him.

God returned Moses so that his mother’s eye would be refreshed, her grief removed, and she would gain witnessed certainty that God’s promise is true. She had already believed this promise, but direct sight of its fulfillment gave certainty. The “promise of Allah” is not restricted to the specific promise to return Moses and make him a messenger; it means God’s unrestricted promise, true without exception. “But most of them do not know” shows that most people do not believe in God’s promises with such certainty and inward trust.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that attaining maturity is the stage at which a person’s strength and faculties intensify, generally considered to occur at eighteen. Istawā means straightness, stability, and firmness; in human life, it is the settled stability a person attains in life’s affairs, normally after maturity though its timing differs among individuals. When Moses reached maturity and this full development, God granted him wisdom and knowledge, as He rewards those who do good.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses entered an Egyptian city while living with Pharaoh, at an hour when people had withdrawn indoors and streets and markets were empty, such as midday or the middle of the night. It infers that Pharaoh’s palace lay outside or at the far end of the city, an inference supported by: And a man came running from the remotest part of the city… (28:20).

The two combatants were an Israelite, one of Moses’ religious followers—though the Children of Israel retained little of their ancestral faith beyond its name and outwardly imitated Pharaoh’s worship—and a Copt, enemy of Moses and the Israelites. The latter identification is also supported by Moses’ words: And they [the Copts] have a crime against me; therefore, I fear that they may slay me (26:14). The Israelite appealed to Moses for aid, and Moses struck the Copt with his fist, causing his death.

The commentary holds that this was accidental homicide, not deliberate murder: fa wakazahu denotes striking or punching with the whole fist, and fa qaḍā ʿalayhi means bringing the man’s affair to an end through death. Had the killing been intentional, the Qur’an would more fittingly have used al-qatl. Moses’ statement, This is on account of Satan’s doing, attributes to Satan the antagonism and fighting that culminated in the death, not a sinful act by Moses. Satan stirred their hostility, drew Moses into the affair, and thereby exposed him to Pharaoh’s and the Copts’ severe retaliation.

Moses recognized that striking the Copt had been an error which brought him into grave danger. Such an error cannot be ascribed to God, who guides to truth and right; it is attributed to Satan, who leads people into not only sin but whatever is contrary to what is right and brings hardship. Moses had defended an Israelite against an unjust unbeliever, so his act was neither sin nor wrongdoing. His words are instead severe self-reproach and regret over a mistaken, harmful course of action. Thus his later reply to Pharaoh’s reproach, I did it then while I was of those unable to see the right course (26:20), denotes error rather than disobedience entailing sin and punishment.
verses.16: Al-Mizan interprets Moses’ admission that he had harmed himself as an acknowledgment that his deed had placed him in danger, not that he had committed a sin. His plea for forgiveness seeks the removal of its harmful consequences—deliverance from grief and from Pharaoh and his people—as indicated by: And you killed a man, then We delivered you from grief (wa qatalta nafsan fa najjaynāka min al-ghamm). (20:40). The prayer resembles Adam and his spouse’s acknowledgment that they had been unjust to themselves and their appeal for forgiveness and mercy (7:23).
verses.17:
Al-Mizan prefers reading the bāʾ in bimā anʿamta, “because Thou hast bestowed a favor,” as causal: in gratitude for God’s favor, Moses promises never to aid a guilty person in his crime. Alternative readings take it as an oath, either with an omitted predicate—swearing to repent or desist—or as an imploring oath asking God’s compassion and protection. These alternatives would make it an oath by something other than God, a form not found elsewhere in the Qur’an.

God’s favor includes protecting Moses from Pharaoh, restoring him to his mother, and accepting his penitence and forgiving him; Moses is understood to have learned of that forgiveness through inspiration, a dream, or something similar. More fundamentally, “favor” (al-niʿmah) denotes divine leadership (al-wilāyah al-ilāhiyya), as the Qur’an applies it to those on the straight path: And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, these are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favors (fa ulāʾika maʿa alladhīna anʿam Allāhu ʿalayhim) from among the prophets and the truthful and the martyrs and the good, and a goodly company are they (4:69). Such people are protected from deviation and divine wrath, as in: Keep us on the right path; the path of those upon whom Thou hast bestowed favors (ṣirāṭ alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim). Not [the path] of those upon whom Thy wrath is brought down, nor of those who go astray. (1:6-7).

Accordingly, the mujrimīn are people such as Pharaoh and his followers, not the Israelite whom Moses aided. Although some interpret the term as those who cause another’s crime, or as persons whose assistance leads to crime, the commentary rejects the implication that helping the Israelite or striking the Copt was a crime for which Moses repented. Moses, being among those on the straight path, could not be led by partisan rage to help a criminal. He was one purified, beyond Satan’s access to seduce or lead astray: And mention Moses in the Book; he was one purified, and he was a messenger, a prophet (19:51). The three repeated statements, “He said,” mark distinct acts: his judgment concerning Satan’s doing, his repentance and supplication, and his promise and firm commitment.
verses.18: Al-Mizan takes Moses’ being “in the city” the following morning to show that he had remained there rather than returned to Pharaoh’s palace. Fearful and watchful of Pharaoh’s expected retaliation, he was surprised when the Israelite who had sought his aid the previous day again cried aloud for help against another Copt. Moses rebuked him as manifestly errant—one departing from reason, wisdom, and rightness—because his continual provocation and fighting against such people could bring only certain evil.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan accepts the view of prominent scholars that the speaker who says, “Moses, do you want to kill me,” is the Israelite who had called for help. Hearing Moses’ rebuke, he mistakenly thought Moses intended to strike him and, frightened, accused him of wanting to kill him as he had killed someone the day before. The Copt then learned that Moses had killed the earlier Copt, reported this to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh and his people conferred and resolved to kill Moses.

The context supports this interpretation and renders the alternative—that the Copt spoke—inconsequential. The verse also critically alludes to the current Torah, which says that both disputants were Israelites: the words of reproach and complaint confirm that the speaker here was the Israelite, not the Copt.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains yaʾtamirūna as consulting, conferring, counselling, or recommending. The man came running from the city’s remotest part, where the narrative suggests Pharaoh’s palace stood beyond the city; the chiefs’ consultation was taking place with Pharaoh and by his command. He warned Moses that they intended to kill him and urged him to leave, further supporting the inference that Pharaoh’s palace lay at the city’s far end.
verses.21: Al-Mizan regards Moses’ fearful departure and prayer for deliverance from the unjust people as evidence that he did not consider the Copt’s killing a crime.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, that tilqāʾa means facing or directing oneself toward something, while sawāʾa al-sabīl means the middle or median path. Midian was a city of Shuʿayb’s people in the direction of Tabūk, on the Red Sea; Marāṣid al-Iṭṭilāʿ describes it as larger than Tabūk and as containing the well from which Moses drew water for Shuʿayb’s sheep. It is also suggested that it lay an eight-night journey from Egypt and beyond Pharaoh’s authority, which explains Moses’ choice of destination. Thus, after leaving Egypt, Moses set out toward Midian without knowing its road and prayed that God would guide him to the median path without deviation.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains that al-dhawd means restraining, barring, or keeping back, so the two women were holding their sheep away from the water and from mingling with the people’s flocks. The men were watering their livestock, and al-riʿāʾu means the shepherds. Moses found the women apart from the men, with no man attending their sheep, and asked their purpose. They replied that their established practice was not to water until the male shepherds had finished and left, because their very aged father could no longer perform the task and they had assumed it.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan says that Moses understood the women’s delay in watering as arising from their chastity, modesty, and veiling, as well as from the men’s encroachment upon their rights; he therefore took the initiative and watered their sheep. He then withdrew to the shade to rest from the intense heat and prayed: My Lord! Surely I stand in need of the good Thou hast sent down to me.

Although most commentators take this prayer as a request for food, the commentary considers it more fitting that the “good” means the bodily strength by which Moses had performed deeds pleasing to God: defending the Israelite, fleeing to Midian, and watering Shuʿayb’s sheep. His need for this divinely bestowed strength also entails need for sustenance that would preserve and increase it. On this reading, the lām prefixed to mā has the sense of ilā, “to” or “toward,” rather than indicating purpose.

It appears that Moses vigilantly directed neither deed nor intention, even when natural desire was involved, except toward God’s pleasure. His prayers after striking the Copt, fleeing Egypt, journeying toward Midian, watering the sheep, and later making his agreement with Shuʿayb display this orientation. The commentary consequently rejects both the view that the lām denotes purpose and the interpretation of khayr as religious good, namely rescue from tyrants, as contrary to the context.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains that humā refers to the two women, and that the indefinite use of istiḥyāʾ emphasizes and honors the chastity evident in the woman’s manner of walking. After Moses related his ordeal, Shuʿayb reassured him that he was safe from Pharaoh and his people, who held no authority over Midian.

The commentary sees this as completing God’s response to Moses’ three invocations: he was delivered from the unjust people, guided to Midian by the median path, and summoned to receive recompense and sustenance after watering Shuʿayb’s sheep. God further increased His favor by providing him with sustenance for ten years and a wife with whom he found peace and tranquility.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan holds that istaʾjirhu and the verbal noun istījār indicate employing Moses for Shuʿayb’s general needs, even if the immediate context concerns tending sheep. “The best of those that you can employ is the strong man, the faithful one” supplies the reason for the command to employ him: Moses should be employed because he is strong and trustworthy. The expression names the cause—the strong, faithful man—in place of its effect, strength and reliability.

The daughter knew Moses’ strength from his watering of the sheep. She inferred his trustworthiness from his chastity and modesty in speaking with the women, watering their sheep, and accompanying her to Shuʿayb. This shows that the daughter who urged Shuʿayb to employ Moses was the same daughter who brought him her father’s invitation; this identification is also transmitted in reports of the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt and is preferred by many commentators.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains Shuʿayb’s words as a proposal that Moses serve him as an employee for eight years, with ten years left to Moses’ voluntary choice, in exchange for marriage to one of Shuʿayb’s daughters. It is not yet a definitive marriage contract, since the particular daughter is not specified; the phrase “one of these two daughters” also shows that both were present.

The term al-ḥijaj means years, being the plural of ḥijjatun; its usage indicates that pilgrimage to God’s House, a practice of Abraham’s shariʿah, was also observed among them. Shuʿayb’s assurance that he did not wish to burden Moses describes the employment as free from hardship and presents him as a virtuous employer. “If Allah pleases, you will find me one of the good” expresses his hope that Moses will find him among the good, not uncertainty about whether he himself will become such.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan identifies the speaker as Moses. By saying that the matter was an agreement between them, Moses confirmed Shuʿayb’s proposed arrangement and required that neither party infringe their mutual covenant. He clarified that the choice between the two terms belonged to him: if he completed eight years, Shuʿayb could not compel him to serve longer; if he served ten, Shuʿayb could not prevent him from completing the additional term.

By making Allah guardian-witness over their words, Moses both called God to attest to the agreement and entrusted to Him any future dispute and its judgment, since testimony and judgment belong to God. The commentary compares this wording with Jacob’s statement: And when they gave him their covenant, he said: Allah is a guardian-witness for what we say (falammā atawhu mawthiqahum qāla Allāhu ʿalā mā naqūlu wakīl, 12:66).
verses.29: Al-Mizan explains that Moses had completed his service to Shuʿayb—reportedly the longer of the two terms—when he travelled with his family. On a bitterly cold night, having lost their way near the mountain, he perceived a fire and told them to wait while he sought either news of the route or jadhwatun min al-nār, a piece of fire, with which they could warm themselves. The parallel wording, “haply I may bring to you therefrom a live coal or find guidance at the fire” (20:10), particularly indicates that they were lost. His plural command umkuthū also shows that, besides his wife, others were travelling with him.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that the blessed spot was a distinct patch of land on the right side of the valley, where the bush stood and from which Moses was called. Al-ayman qualifies the side as the right, rather than meaning auspicious. The place was blessed through divine proximity and speech, and sacred enough that Moses was commanded to remove his shoes: “Therefore put off your shoes; you are in the sacred valley, Ṭuwā (20:12).”

The bush was, in one respect, the source from which the divine call arose, but God’s speech was not located or inherent in it as human speech inheres in a speaker. Rather, the bush was a veil through which God spoke to Moses in a manner befitting His sanctity, though God truly encompasses all things. This accords with: “And it is not for any mortal that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger and revealing by His permission what He pleases; He is High, Wise (42:51).” The commentary rejects both the claim that speech must occupy a location and the claim that this was the highest prophetic mode of communication: speech from behind the bush was mediated by a veil, whereas the cited verse apparently places unmediated revelation above communication through either veil or messenger.

“I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds” identifies the transcendent God by the name Allah and affirms the exclusive unity of His lordship. As Master and governor of the whole universe, He alone deserves worship; nothing falls under another’s independent authority so that another lord or god could exist. The statement thus succinctly contains the call elaborated in Sūrah al-Ṭāhā through monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection.
verses.31: Al-Mizan reads the address, “O Moses! Come forward and fear not; you are of those who are secure,” as containing the implied sense, “It was said to him.” It assures Moses that he is a messenger, and that messengers are secure in God’s presence and are not liable to rebuke or censure. It thereby clarifies: “O Moses! Fear not; the messengers shall not fear in My presence (27:10).”
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses was commanded to insert his hand into the opening of his bosom, whence it would emerge white without al-sūʾ, apparently meaning without leprosy. This qualification apparently alludes critically to the present-day Torah’s account that his hand came out “whitely leprous like snow.” Al-rahb means fear, while al-janāḥ may mean the hand or upper arm and shoulder.

The commentary rejects interpretations that connect “draw your hand to yourself to ward off fear” directly to Moses’ fright at the staff becoming a serpent—whether gathering his hands to his chest to dispel inward fear, or ceasing to stretch out his arms in warding off the snake. The intervening, unconnected command concerning the white hand separates the two statements. It is also suggested that the command urges resolve in carrying out messengership, lest fear impede God’s purpose. Yet it is not implausible that it instructs Moses in modesty and humility: the proud draw their arms away from their sides in self-exaltation, whereas the command may resemble the instruction to Muḥammad, “and make yourself gentle to the believers (15:88).” The staff and white hand are the two arguments from God to Pharaoh and his chiefs, who are a transgressing people.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says that Moses refers to his killing of the Copt with the whole of his fist and fears that the Copts will kill him in retaliation.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains that a ridʾ is one who aids another and strengthens his back. Moses asks for Aaron because Aaron is more eloquent, not because Aaron’s presence would prevent the Copts from rejecting Moses; one prepared to belie Moses would also belie Aaron. Rather, Moses fears that their rejection will anger him and, owing to his stutter, prevent him from clearly expressing his proof. As “He said: O my Lord! Surely I fear that they will reject me, and my breast straitens, and my tongue is not eloquent; therefore, send Thou Aaron [to help me] (26:12-13)” shows, Aaron is to help clarify and verify Moses’ truthfulness when the Copts dispute with him.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s promise to strengthen Moses’ arm through Aaron means that Aaron will fortify and aid him. “So that they shall not reach you” means the Copts will be unable to overcome the two, whether by killing them or otherwise. God will grant them authority, dominance, and triumph through His signs; the concluding promise shows that this supremacy extends to Moses, Aaron, and those who follow them.

The commentary accordingly takes sulṭān here to mean domination and victory. It notes an alternative that takes it as al-ḥujja, conclusive proof that leaves no excuse; on that reading, “due to Our signs” attaches to “you two and those who follow you shall be uppermost,” rather than to “so that they shall not reach you.”
verses.36: Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh’s people called Moses’ extraordinary divine signs “forged enchantment”: magic he had fabricated and falsely attributed to God. Their further statement, “we have never heard of this from our fathers of old,” more probably concerns his religious call, not the signs. The repeated hādhā indicates two distinct referents, and their claim elsewhere that they could produce comparable magic shows that lack of a precedent for magic would not prevent them from calling it such. Their objection was therefore that Moses had brought an innovated religion unknown among their forefathers, a reading that accords with Moses’ response in the following verse.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan takes Moses’ statement as a challenge and refutation of Pharaoh’s people when they claimed that his call was unknown to their forefathers. Moses refers to himself as the one sent by the Lord of the universe with guidance—his call to monotheism—whose clear signs prove that it comes from God, and whose followers have been promised a good end.

“The good end of the abode” may mean Paradise, worldly inheritance, or both this world and the hereafter. The commentary prefers the comprehensive sense, followed by the worldly one, especially since Moses adds that the unjust will not prosper. He thus exposes Pharaoh and his people: their tyrannical order, which departs from the social justice to which human nature and the cosmos conform, cannot have the good end. Although some exegetes take the statement as merely joined to the Egyptians’ rejection so listeners may compare the two claims, the commentary holds that its refutational sense better suits the context.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains Pharaoh’s words as an attempt to expose Moses as a liar by dismissing both his call and its miraculous signs. His claim that he knew no god for the people besides himself feigns fairness and honesty in order to gain the chiefs’ acceptance. It is a rhetorical exclusion: Moses affirmed divinity for God alone and denied it to all others, while Pharaoh denied it to God and asserted it for himself; the verse does not address the other deities worshipped by Pharaoh and his people.

Pharaoh orders Hāmān to fire clay into bricks and build a lofty ṣarḥ, a tower or palace. By seeking knowledge of “Moses’ Allah,” he may mean that he wishes to ascend and look toward the heavens, assuming God to be embodied and located in a heavenly region. Alternatively, he may simply seek to deceive and confuse the people, or intend an observation point from which to inspect the heavens for evidence of Moses’ mission. The parallel account—“And the Pharaoh said: O Hāmān! Build for me a tower that I may attain the means of access—the means of access to the heavens—then reach the Allah of Moses, and I think him to be a liar… (40:36-37)”—supports the first possibility.

His ending, “I think him to be one of the liars,” marks a movement from professed ignorance to supposing God’s nonexistence. Yet Pharaoh was lying and trying to mislead his people, for Moses had told him: “Truly you know that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent down these as clear proof… (17:102).” The interpretation that Pharaoh merely denied God by denying knowledge of Him does not accord with the verse’s ending.
verses.39: Al-Mizan says that Pharaoh and his hosts were unjustly proud and, inwardly, were convinced that they would not return to God, although they denied this unjustly and arrogantly.
verses.40: Al-Mizan explains that al-nabdh means casting or throwing, and al-yamm means the sea or great waters. The verse’s description of Pharaoh and his hosts being cast into the sea treats them with scorn and makes their punishment frighteningly alarming.
verses.41: Al-Mizan explains “calling to the Fire” either as a call to disbelief and disobedience that merits its punishment or, by naming the effect for its cause, as a call to what leads there. God’s making them Imams means rendering them precursors in deviation for later generations to follow, not the first inventors of disbelief. The proposal that “made” merely means “named” or “designated” conflicts with the succeeding verse and uses al-jaʿl unacceptably. Their lack of assistance on the Day of Resurrection means that no helper’s intercession will benefit them.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that because Pharaoh and his people were leaders calling others to the Fire and serving as examples in disbelief and disobedience, they continue to bear the effects and burdens of the later deviation of those who follow them. A curse therefore pursues them continuously as long as such disbelief and disobedience endure, in the sense of: “And most certainly they shall carry their own burdens, and other burdens with their own burdens… (29:13)” and “And We write down what they have sent before and their footprints… (36:12).”

The indefiniteness of laʿnah indicates its intensity and continuity. Denied any helper’s intercession on the Day of Resurrection, they will also be made repulsive: souls will abhor them, people will flee from them, and none will approach them.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan identifies Moses’ Book as the Torah, revealed to him by God; the lām in wa laqad ātaynā intensifies an elided oath. Its coming after the destruction of earlier generations—possibly including Pharaoh’s people—indicates the pressing need to renew the divine call after teachings had been lost. The Book also recalls the histories and punishments of those who denied God’s signs, so that people may reflect and take heed.

It calls the Torah baṣāʾira li al-nās, clear proofs by which people perceive the truth and distinguish it from falsehood; hudan, that by which they are guided to right knowledge; and raḥmah, through obedience to whose laws they become worthy of mercy. Thus, after the destruction of former peoples, wisdom required a renewed Book that would furnish proof, guidance, and mercy, reminding humanity of its obligatory beliefs and deeds.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse addresses the Prophet Muḥammad and denies that he was present when the Torah was revealed to Moses. Al-gharbī qualifies an elided “valley” or “mountain,” so the location is the side of the western valley or western mountain, rather than merely a western side.

The revealed “commandment” includes a covenant concerning the rules of prophethood conveyed in the Torah; the covenant concerning Moses’ messengership is indicated later by the call at the mountain. “You were not among the witnesses” reiterates that the Prophet neither attended nor witnessed this revelation.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that generations were raised after Moses and a long period elapsed for them. Although the Prophet was not present to witness the events, God revealed to him Moses’ story and the account of the Book given to Moses; this is concisely implied by the verse’s wording.

Nor did the Prophet reside among the people of Midian—Shuʿayb and his people—while Moses was there. Rather, God sent him as a messenger to his own people and revealed these signs to him so that he might recite to the Meccan polytheists the account of Moses’ time in Midian.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan takes the “call” to be God’s call to Moses from the bush or tree on the night Moses saw the fire by the mountain of al-Ṭūr. The Prophet was not present when God called, spoke to, and chose Moses for messengership; God informed him of it instead as a mercy.

The shift from God’s first-person speech to “a mercy from your Lord” displays His complete care for the Prophet. The people to be warned are apparently the Prophet’s contemporaries, perhaps together with their forefathers, since prophets such as Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, and Ishmael had long passed away. The purpose is that they may take heed.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that “what their hands have sent before” means the sins and evils they earned through their beliefs and conduct. The muṣībah that would strike them is not confined to this world or the next, for disbelief and immorality bring divine punishment in both.

The verse implies that, were it not for their potential argument against God if no messenger had been sent, He would not have sent one. Otherwise, when punished for their disbelief and immorality, they could say that had a messenger come, they would have followed God’s communications and become believers.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that the truth brought to them was the Prophet Muḥammad’s mission and the Qur’an revealed to him. Their demand that he receive what Moses received suggests that they wanted the Qur’an to be revealed all at once, as they say elsewhere: And those who disbelieve say: Why has not the Qur’an been revealed to him all at once? (25:32)

Their earlier disbelief in what Moses received is expressed by calling the Qur’an and Torah “Two [works of] magic backing up each other.” This denies faith in the two Books themselves. Their further statement, “Surely we are unbelievers in all,” denies the very principle of prophethood; this distinction apparently accounts for the repeated “they say.”
verses.49:
Al-Mizan holds that the challenge to bring a Book from Allah better in guidance than the Qur’an and Torah rests on the necessity that God provide humanity with a guiding Book and messenger, whom people are obliged to follow. If the two Books were false magic, the truth would have to be found in another Book; the opponents must therefore produce one superior in guidance if their accusation is true.

In this debate, the verse establishes that the Qur’an and the Torah together are guiding Books and that no Book surpasses them. Although the Qur’an states that corruption and defect entered the present Torah, the Torah intended here is the original revealed to Moses, which the Qur’an confirms; together with the Qur’an, it is the subject under consideration. “If you are truthful” concerns their claim that the two are magic supporting one another.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that if the challengers cannot produce a Book better in guidance than the Qur’an and Torah yet continue to reject them as magic, they are not seeking truth or following what reason clearly establishes; they are following their low desires. It is also possible that the verse means they have founded their whole way of life on whim, disbelieving in prophethood and in revealed divine instruction that must govern life. The latter reading is perhaps supported by what follows.

The rhetorical question declares that none is more astray than one who follows desire without guidance from Allah. Following desire diverts a person from truth and guidance, and is therefore injustice; Allah does not guide the unjust, and one deprived of guidance is lost.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that God repeatedly conveyed the Qur’an to the Meccan polytheists in connected, successive revelation: verses and sūrahs followed one another, bringing promises, warnings, laws, narratives, lessons, judgments, and admonition so that they might remember.

It understands the pronouns in “those whom We gave the Book before it, they are believers in it” as referring to the Qur’an, rather than the Prophet Muḥammad, because this better suits the context. The verse begins praise of a particular group among the People of the Book who believed in the Qur’an, following the censure of the Meccan polytheists; it does not concern all believing People of the Book generally.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains that God repeatedly conveyed the Qur’an to the Meccan polytheists in connected, successive revelation: verses and sūrahs followed one another, bringing promises, warnings, laws, narratives, lessons, judgments, and admonition so that they might remember.

It understands the pronouns in “those whom We gave the Book before it, they are believers in it” as referring to the Qur’an, rather than the Prophet Muḥammad, because this better suits the context. The verse begins praise of a particular group among the People of the Book who believed in the Qur’an, following the censure of the Meccan polytheists; it does not concern all believing People of the Book generally.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan understands the singular pronouns as referring to the Qur’an. When it is recited to the believing People of the Book, they affirm it as the definite truth from their Lord, a truth they already recognize. Their statement, “we were submitters before this,” means either that they submitted to it before its revelation or that they already believed in the religion to which the Qur’an calls, namely Islām.

Although the pronouns have also been taken to refer to the Prophet Muḥammad, the first interpretation better accords with the context. In either case, they refer to what these People of the Book had read in their scriptures concerning the Prophet’s attributes and the Book to be revealed to him, as indicated by Those who follow the Messenger-Prophet, the ummī, whom they find written down with them in the Torah and the Evangel… (7:157) and Is it not a sign to them that the learned men of the Israelites know it? (26:197).
verses.54:
Al-Mizan says that the believing People of the Book are promised a double reward: for faith in their own scripture and for faith in the Qur’an, and for the patience required by this faith and its struggle against desire. An alternative interpretation makes the reward for patience in their religion and for harm and hardship inflicted by unbelievers, but the context favors the former.

Their repelling evil with good is best understood, in context, as meeting the hot-tempered impetuosity of others with forbearance (al-ḥilm). They avert people’s hurt and harm through patient indulgence; they also spend from what God has provided them.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan defines al-laghw here as idle and unworthy speech—gibberish, excessive talk, insults, and crude or coarse words. When the believing People of the Book hear it, they turn away and do not answer evil with its like.

Their words, “We shall have our deeds and you shall have your deeds,” suspend hostilities. “Peace be on you” assures the speakers of safety from them and marks an honorable departure, like: And the servants of the Beneficent Allah are they who walk on the earth in humbleness, and when the ignorant address them, they say: Peace (25:63). “We do not desire the ignorant” means that they do not seek association or social intercourse with such people; it confirms their refusal to answer evil with evil.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan distinguishes the guidance denied to the Prophet from merely showing the right path. The guidance meant is bringing a person to the intended destination, so that the heart overflows with faith; this belongs exclusively to Allah. A messenger can nevertheless point out and indicate the path. Al-ihtidāʾ means accepting true guidance.

The verse concludes the contrast between the Prophet’s own polytheist people, who followed desire and rejected revealed truth, and the People of the Book who acknowledged it. Guidance is God’s affair: He may guide people outside the Prophet’s community, while not guiding members of his own people whom he wishes to accept guidance. Allah knows best who follows the right way.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains that the Meccan polytheists’ fear of being “carried off” from their land figuratively means murder, captivity, and plunder, by which they, their families, and their property would be taken and Mecca lost to them. Their excuse for refusing faith was that the idolatrous Arabs would not tolerate their rejection of idols. Yet by calling the Prophet’s message “the guidance,” they implicitly acknowledged the truth of the call and its Book; fear of expulsion alone restrained them.

The verse gives the first reply to this excuse: God Himself settled them in Mecca, a sacred territory safe because the Arabs revered it. Thus they had no reason to fear expulsion if they believed. Its abundant, varied fruits are gathered there as sustenance from God, also removing any fear that belief would cut off their provisions. Most do not know this, imagining instead that their security depends on their polytheism and idol-worship.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains that towns destroyed after exulting arrogantly and ungratefully in their material means of life were oppressive and tyrannical. Their ruined, visible dwellings remained uninhabited after them, except for a few dwellings; the exception is more suitably connected with the dwellings themselves than with a brief period of later habitation.

God is called their inheritor because, after destroying their rebellious possessors, He remained while their dwellings remained without them. In truth He was always their absolute owner; their ownership and control were only nominal and permitted by Him. Their disappearance merely manifested His real sovereignty. The verse therefore answers the Meccans’ excuse: refusing guidance cannot secure the continuance of their land, ease, or safety, for many prosperous and self-exultant peoples were destroyed and left no inheritor but God.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that umm al-qurā is the principal, central town to which surrounding towns turn. God does not annihilate towns until He has first established decisive proof by raising a messenger in their central town to recite His communications, and until their people have shown themselves unjust by rejecting those signs and belying the messenger.

Coming after the warning about destroyed towns, the verse threatens the Meccan polytheists: a messenger has been sent in their central city, Mecca, and if they persist in belying him, they acquire the conditions for divine punishment. The shift to “your Lord” both strengthens the Prophet and affirms his conclusive proof; the return to “We” resumes the preceding mode of discourse.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that everything granted to people is merely enjoyment and adornment of the finite, perishing worldly life. What is with Allah is the enduring bliss and reward of the hereafter, gained through following guidance and believing in God’s signs, and is therefore better and more lasting.

This is the third answer to the Meccans’ fear of expulsion. Even if following guidance meant losing their land, what they would lose would only be transient worldly enjoyment, whereas what is with God is everlasting. They should therefore prefer the latter.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse rebukingly denies any equivalence between one who follows guidance and meets God’s unfailing goodly promise—forgiveness and paradise—and one who confines himself to worldly adornment and is deprived of that promise. The latter will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection for punishment or questioning, censure, and reproach.

The verse begins the clarification of why guidance is better than worldly enjoyment: the follower of guidance meets the promised good, while the worldly person will face summons, the dissociation and non-response of those he worshiped, punishment, and questioning about his response to the messengers.
verses.62: Al-Mizan explains that the shurakāʾ are the deities whom the Meccan polytheists worshiped. They were called God’s associates because the polytheists assigned them prerogatives belonging only to God, including worship and the management of the universe.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan distinguishes two kinds of beings made associates of God: honored servants of God, such as angels and Jesus son of Mary; and rebellious beings, including jinn, human claimants to divinity, Satan and his cohorts, and leaders followed in falsehood. “Those against whom the sentence has become confirmed” refers to the second kind, for they confess that they led others astray and disclaim their worshipers. They are the objects of polytheism and agents of misguidance, even though those who worshiped them had lost them at that station.

Their statement means that the polytheists’ error resembled their own: just as these leaders erred freely and without coercion, their followers also chose error freely. They neither compelled the followers’ misguidance nor removed their free will. Their declaration of being clear of them is thus an absolute dissociation: “it was not us that they worshiped” means that the worship was not coerced by them, and they disclaim responsibility for those deeds. The suggestions that the followers really worshiped their own whims or the satans are not credible.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains that the polytheists are commanded to summon the deities they claimed as God’s associates, so that those gods might help them and repel the punishment. The associate-gods do not answer, and the polytheists then see the punishment.

“Would that they had followed the right way” may be understood through an omitted conditional consequence: had they followed guidance, they would have known the punishment to be true. It may also simply express the wish that they had followed the right way.
verses.65: Al-Mizan connects this question to (28:62). After the polytheists are asked about the alleged associates of God and reproachfully directed to seek their aid, they are asked what answer they gave to the messengers sent by God, who called them to faith and virtuous deeds.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains that the discourse becoming obscure to the polytheists means that they are overwhelmed on every side on the Day of Resurrection: all avenues and means of influence are cut off, and they find no excuse with which to avert punishment for rejecting the messengers. Consequently, they cannot consult one another to devise a defence for their denial.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains that the preceding wretched description concerns those who disbelieve and do not repent. One who repents to God, believes, and performs virtuous deeds may be among the successful. The ʿasā may express certain attainment in accordance with the usage of the noble, or hope and expectation on the part of the repentant person; such a person should anticipate salvation and success.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan presents this as the fourth reply to the Meccan polytheists’ refusal of guidance. Creation belongs solely to God; every supposed influence is either His creature, whose existence and effects depend on Him, or an impossibility. Nothing can compel Him, prevent His act, or repel His decree. He therefore creates freely as He wills.

The same unrestricted prerogative belongs to Him in legislation. Human nature reaches righteousness, perfection, and happiness through what God commands and avoids what He forbids; thus He alone chooses the laws and obligations by which human beings are to be guided. “Your Lord creates” denotes His unrestricted choice in creation, while “chooses what He pleases” chiefly denotes His choice in moral legislation, which follows creation. The following negation, “to choose is not theirs,” confirms this legislative choice for God and denies it to human beings.

Human beings do possess volition in their acts, though their acts depend on many external causes, all ultimately terminating in God, who created them with this capacity. They are also free among their fellow human beings unless they voluntarily surrender some freedom—for example, by entering a society governed by its laws, making an agreement of submission, or hiring out their work. Yet God possesses both their selves and their acts absolutely, through creative and legislative ownership. Therefore they have no choice against what He chooses for them in command or prohibition, just as they have none against His creative will, even when His choice displeases them.

God’s transcendence above their associates includes His transcendence above the polytheistic claim that they may accept or reject what He has chosen. Such a claim of independent choice entails claiming independence from God and associating another with Him in divinity. By saying “your Lord,” the verse also supports the Prophet: the command sent through him has gone forth and is not subject to their rejection. “Glory be to Allah” explicitly declares the transcendence of God, the origin of all things, from every imperfection.
verses.69: Al-Mizan explains that God knows both what hearts conceal and what people manifest. It is perhaps for this reason that the verse follows the preceding one: God chose for them with knowledge of the inward and outward filth of their polytheism and disobedience, and in His wisdom purified them from it.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan takes “He” to refer to “your Lord”: He alone is Allah, uniquely distinguished by divinity, and there is no god besides Him. Since He knows their inward and outward state and chooses for them to worship Him alone, they must worship Him alone as the sole being worthy of worship.

“All praise is due to Him in this [life] and the hereafter” establishes this because every perfection and blessing comes from God’s essential perfection, and every praiseworthy quality in anything else ultimately returns to Him. Since worship is praise in word or deed, He alone deserves worship. “His is the judgment” means that, as absolute owner in creation and legislation, He decrees that His servants worship none but Him. “To Him you shall be brought back” means that He alone will reckon and reward them; since religion belongs to Him alone, worship belongs to Him alone.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains al-sarmad as endless, continuous perpetuity, here describing night until the Day of Resurrection, after which there is no night. The challenge asks which god besides Allah could oppose His decision by bringing even light, through which people may see and seek their livelihood.

Although the contrast might have been expected to ask who could bring day after perpetual night, light is mentioned because it is the easier demand: if another god managed the universe, let it bring even light. Its inability makes the exclusiveness of God’s power clearer. The corresponding question about perpetual day asks who could bring night rather than merely darkness, because only sufficient, extensive darkness is night and permits rest. The indefinite ḍiyāʾ reinforces the challenge. “Do you not then hear?” calls for reflective hearing that recognizes there is no god besides God.
verses.72: Al-Mizan explains that the night brought after perpetual day is the time in which people rest and recover from the fatigue of seeking livelihood by day. “Do you not then see?” calls for sight joined with understanding and recollection. The pairing of “hear” for perpetual night and “see” for perpetual day is fitting, especially because daylight accords with sight.
verses.73: Al-Mizan presents the verse as the conclusion to the preceding proof. Out of His mercy, God made the night for rest and the day for seeking His grace, while gratitude concerns both night and day. Their creation, the benefits of rest and seeking provision, and the laws that guide people toward gratitude are all effects of God’s mercy.
verses.74: Al-Mizan says that this repeats the earlier question about the alleged associates because the following verse depends on its meaning.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains that, on the Day of Resurrection, a witness of deeds will be drawn from every umma, understood simply as a group of people. The verse does not specify that this witness is necessarily the prophet sent to that community, though a prophet may be an instance of such a witness. The polytheists will be challenged to produce decisive proof that God has associates.

Their fabrication—that associates share in divinity and worship—will vanish, and they will know that divinity belongs solely to God. Although some interpret this as their failure to produce proof, requiring the clauses to be reversed, Al-Mizan holds that the Day of Resurrection is rather the unmediated manifestation of truth: every falsehood that had obscured it is removed, so their fabrication necessarily disappears and God’s unity and divinity become evident, not merely rationally inferred from their lack of proof.

Al-ḥaqq may also be a verbal noun: God may be the Truth Himself, if truth is identical with His essence; or truth may terminate in and subsist through Him, if it is other than Him.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that Qārūn was one of the Children of Israel, but committed al-baghyu against them: he behaved haughtily and tyrannically, infringed their rights, and wronged them. Allah had given him treasures whose keys, not the treasure-chests themselves—as some commentators wrongly held—would weigh down a strong ʿuṣba. The more suitable sense of nāʾa bi is that the burden made its bearers bend under its weight. An ʿuṣba is a cooperating group, and the description of Joseph’s nine brothers as an ʿuṣba rules out proposed numerical definitions incompatible with that usage.

The prohibition, “Do not exult,” concerns al-farḥ: rejoicing in wealth in a manner that produces pride, conceit, and ingratitude for Allah’s favors. Excessive delight in worldly wealth attaches one to this life, makes one forget the hereafter, and breeds arrogant exultation; thus Allah does not love the exultant.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that seeking the future abode through what Allah has given means using one’s wealth in Allah’s service and in ways that earn His pleasure. “Do not neglect your portion of this world” means neither abandoning one’s allotted worldly sustenance nor failing to strive in this life for the hereafter, for the lasting share of the world is the good one does there for the hereafter.

It also gives a very good complementary interpretation: even the prosperous person’s actual share is only what he consumes and wears, while the surplus is a grace left to others; he should take what suffices and give the excess in kindness. Doing good to others therefore means spending benevolently from wealth Allah gave without its recipient deserving or requiring it. One must not use wealth, rank, or influence to cause mischief, for Allah does not love corrupters and creation is founded upon goodness and reform.
verses.78:
Al-Mizan takes Qārūn’s statement, “I have been given this only on account of the knowledge I have,” as his reply to believers who had told him that his wealth was Allah’s gracious gift and should be used to seek the hereafter, benefit others, and avoid arrogant corruption. He instead claimed that his exclusive knowledge of acquiring and managing wealth made him deserving of it. On that premise, he treated the wealth as an independent right, to use for his comforts, authority, and desires.

The commentary regards this as the common human delusion that personal intelligence, competence, and experience—not divine providence and favorable circumstances—are the effective cause of one’s wealth, power, and standing. Like the attitude described in (39:49-52) and (40:82-83), Qārūn’s appeal to “knowledge” deliberately avoids acknowledging Allah’s beneficence and belittles His greatness.

The question about earlier generations stronger and wealthier than he is a rebuke that refutes his claim. If knowledge and amassed power truly secured wealth and warded off harm, those destroyed generations would have defended themselves and continued to enjoy what they possessed. “And the guilty shall not be asked about their faults” describes Allah’s manner of punishment: because He knows the reality of their crimes, He need not question them or allow them respite to devise excuses, display prepared humility or repentance, and avert punishment. Unlike human authorities, Allah can suddenly overwhelm the guilty without their knowledge.

Al-Mizan reports but rejects as unfitting to the context interpretations that identify Qārūn’s knowledge as mastery of the Torah, alchemy, extracting hidden treasures, Allah’s knowledge of him, or a blessing taught by Allah. Related proposals take ʿalā in ūtītuhu ʿalā ʿilmin ʿindī either as superiority in knowledge or as causal “on account of” knowledge. It likewise finds contextually unsuitable the view that the absence of questioning concerns the Day of Resurrection—whether questioning means rebuke rather than inquiry, occurs at a different station, or distinguishes ordinary sinners from especially wicked ones.
verses.79: Al-Mizan explains that al-ḥaẓẓ is a share of happiness, fortune, or good luck. Those who wished for Qārūn’s finery and wealth had made the life of this world their sole aim; consequently, they were ignorant of the hereafter and of the reward Allah has prepared for His servants. They therefore regarded his wealth as mighty good fortune in an absolute, unqualified sense.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains that “Woe to you!” is not here an invocation of destruction, but a warning intended to restrain the ignorant believers who wished for Qārūn’s fortune. The believers given knowledge of Allah tell them that Allah’s reward is better than Qārūn’s wealth for the one who believes and does good; if they truly possessed faith and virtue, they would seek that reward instead.

“None is made to receive this except the patient” may mean that only the patient understand and receive the statement that Allah’s reward is better, or that only they understand and successfully follow this way of conduct. Such patience includes endurance in adversity, obedience to Allah, and resisting disobedience. Recognizing and acting on the superiority of the hereafter requires bearing the bitterness of opposing one’s nature, whims, desires, and the rebellious prompting of the soul.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that the earth’s swallowing Qārūn and his abode was the consequence of his rebellion and intransigence. He had no party able to repel Allah’s punishment, nor could he defend himself. Neither his accumulated wealth nor the power he thought he had gained through knowledge protected or benefited him.

His destruction thus made the falsity of his claims manifest: he had imagined that he merited his wealth, could dispense with Allah, and could secure good and avert evil through his own intellectual genius, power, and riches. In reality, Allah was the One who had given him what he possessed.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that the particle way in the speech of those who had desired Qārūn’s position most readily conveys remorse, regret, and repentance, though it may also express wonder. They now acknowledge the falsity of the claim they had previously endorsed: wealth, power, and abundance do not arise independently from human intelligence and management, but Allah enlarges or restricts provision for whom He pleases. Their statement that Allah would otherwise have abased them expresses this realization with certainty; waykaʾanna rhetorically indicates the beginning of doubt about their former conviction. Their final regret that the ungrateful never prosper seeks to escape the implication of having wished to be in Qārūn’s place.

The commentary treats the future abode as the outcome of the story. The distant demonstrative tilka signals the honor and lofty rank of the blissful abode of the hereafter, namely paradise. It is specifically assigned to those who do not seek superiority over Allah’s servants through arrogance and do not seek corruption through disobedience. Since Allah’s path accords with the requirements of human creation, every disobedience causes corruption directly or indirectly; seeking superiority is itself a particularly noted instance of this corruption. The verse’s general promise is qualified by the avoidance of grave sins. In context, “the good end” is the blessed abode of the hereafter rather than prosperity in both worlds.
