verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains that whoever brings good receives more than it through Allah’s grace, whereas the doers of evil are not punished beyond what they did; this is perfect justice, just as the multiplication of good is perfect grace. The plural wording, “those who do [much] evil,” together with “what they were doing,” perhaps indicates those persistently engulfed in sins. One who has mingled good with evil may, however, be forgiven.

Good and evil are judged by their effect upon the human being, and recompense concerns that effect rather than the outward constituent of an act, which is merely movement. This also answers the question of how monotheism can receive something better than itself. Either the verse concerns non-creedal matters, or, if applied to monotheism, its reward can still exceed the deed because monotheism has stronger and weaker degrees; a deficient degree receives a reward greater than it.
verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains that faraḍa ʿalayka al-Qurʾān means making the Qur’an binding upon the Prophet. It can mean obliging him to practise and implement its laws, but the better interpretation is that he is obliged to recite it, convey it, and act by it, because this accords with the promised return that follows.

Maʿād, derived from “returning,” may be a place or time of return. It has been interpreted as Mecca, death, resurrection or its plain, the praiseworthy station and great intercession, paradise, Bayt al-Maqdis in a promised second miʿrāj, or a beloved affair; most or all of these may be valid applications. Yet the sūrah’s context chiefly presents the verse as the promised fulfillment intimated by Moses’ and the Children of Israel’s story. As God rescued them from Pharaoh’s humiliation, established their dignity and power, and gave Moses the Torah, He revealed the Qur’an to guide and complete the proof despite Meccan denial, and promises the believers deliverance, the triumph of their religion, and settlement after oppression.

Thus, the One who bound the Prophet to recite, proclaim, and practise the Qur’an will return him to a destination that is truly his place of return, as the Torah raised Moses and his people. The return is realized in the Prophet’s triumphant return to Mecca after migration: the religion was established, idols were broken, polytheism was destroyed, and formerly oppressed believers inherited the land. The indefiniteness of maʿād indicates the sublime greatness of this return, incomparable to his former residence in Mecca.

“My Lord knows best him who has brought the guidance and him who is in manifest error” confirms this reading by echoing Moses’ response to Pharaoh’s people when they called his signs magic. The Prophet is commanded to answer his own polytheist deniers as Moses answered Pharaoh’s people, for their prophetic experiences are completely alike. The verse alludes only to the first part of Moses’ statement because its promise of the Prophet’s maʿād completes the indication. “Him who has brought the guidance” is the Prophet, and “him who is in manifest error” his polytheist people; the contrast is between their error and what he brought, because their denial was directed chiefly against his message rather than his person.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan takes the verse first as confirmation of the preceding promise: God will unexpectedly return the Prophet to his destination just as He unexpectedly inspired the Book to him. It may also be a renewed reminder of God’s blessings upon him. The Book was not an ordinary, anticipated occurrence, but a special mercy from his Lord; the promised advancement and ultimate success of his call likewise require him to persevere diligently.

Because the revelation was an unanticipated divine favor, the Prophet must dissociate himself from the unbelievers: he must neither support nor obey them, must call exclusively to his Lord, and must not be among the polytheists. The definite exception in “but it is a mercy from your Lord” stresses that this inspiration was not something that could have been hoped for or expected, and “therefore, be not a backer of the unbelievers” follows from that favor. It is highly probable that this prohibition parallels Moses’ pledge, after God had favored him with judgment and knowledge, never to support the guilty. The Book was given to the Prophet so that he might guide people to truth and monotheism; he therefore must neither aid the unbelievers’ rejection nor incline to them or be diverted by them from God’s revealed signs. The following verse explains this command.

In a grammatical note on the preceding expression rabbī aʿlamu man jāʾa bi al-hudā, Al-Mizan rejects treating aʿlamu as an active participle governing man. While some posit an implied verb, it maintains that man is accusative through the suppressed preposition bi: rabbī aʿlamu bi-man jāʾa bi al-hudā.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is forbidden to be turned away from God’s revealed signs by the unbelievers’ verbal efforts to hinder and dissuade him. The construction resembles the warning to Adam and his wife not to let Satan drive them from the Garden: it commands vigilance lest their action become the cause of one’s turning away.

This verse and the next clarify “therefore be not a backer of the unbelievers” (28:86) by successively emphasizing three commands. First, the Prophet must not turn from the Qur’an despite the polytheists’ claims that it was magic, poetry, soothsaying, or written ancient tales. Next, he must call people to his Lord. Finally, he must not be among the polytheists, meaning those who associate other gods with God. The repeated attribution of al-rabb to the Prophet indicates his special divine mercy and favor, and his distinctive worship of God, which the polytheists do not share.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains that the prohibition against calling on another god restates and clarifies the command not to be among the polytheists. “There is no Allah but He” expresses sincere faith and devotion, for no other being deserves worship, and it also explains why everything other than Him is perishable.

“Thing” includes every existent, and halāk can mean perishing, becoming nonexistent, or becoming void and ineffective. Wajh is what enables a thing to turn toward, meet, or be connected with another. With respect to God, it signifies that by which He turns to creatures and by which they turn to Him: His noble attributes—such as life, power, knowledge, hearing, and sight—His acts of creating, sustaining, giving life and death, forgiving, and showing mercy, and His signs that point to Him. On this reading, every thing is essentially void and has reality only through the grace God grants it. Idols have only their material existence; their alleged divinity and power to benefit or harm are imaginary names coined by worshippers. Likewise, creatures and the social distinctions people ascribe to themselves—power, authority, nobility, wealth, glory, offspring, and support—are perishable mirages. What is truly established is God’s attributes and signs, while all else subsists through His sacred Essence.

Accordingly, the true deity must possess a reality that cannot perish or be voided and must hold the management of the universe. Nothing besides Him has independent authority, even though idolaters regarded their supposed gods as independent managers and therefore worshipped them. Al-Mizan then considers a more accurate interpretation: wajh may mean the very essence or being of a thing. On either this sense or the sense of a noble self, every being other than God is contingent and, in itself, subject to nonexistence; only God is necessary in His essence and existence. The Creator cannot be separated from the manager of creation, so it is senseless to suppose that one being creates while another independently administers affairs. The polytheists’ claim that God is too exalted to be directly worshipped, requiring mediation through angels or others close to Him, is also rejected: valid worship requires cognizance of God, not comprehensive knowledge of Him.

If hālik instead refers to future annihilation, the verse does not mean an absolute extinction after existence, which clear Qur’anic verses negate. Perishing may be the end of a temporal existence, or the stripping away of an initial mode of existence through transfer to a subsequent existence, return to God, and settlement with Him. If wajh means God’s attributes, everything returns to God while His attributes, the inexhaustible sources of His grace, remain without interruption. If it means His sacred Being, everything meets perishing by returning to Him, while His established Being, including His attributes, is untouched by annihilation. In either case, only He can be God.

The objection that paradise, hell, and the Throne would then perish is answered by distinguishing this transformation from absolute destruction. Paradise and hell endure forever, and the Throne is included with them on the basis of traditions identifying it as paradise’s roof. The perishing at issue concerns beings whose initial existence is worldly; it does not characterize the hereafter or realities that are with God, such as the treasures of His mercy and the Preserved Tablet.

Wajh may also mean God’s intended direction—the object toward which one directs oneself—and thereby encompass whatever is exclusively ascribed to Him: His names and attributes, His prophets and messengers, His vice-regents, and His religion. If traditions that specify wajh as “religion” are taken as a specification rather than merely an application, then halāk means corruption and loss of effect: every religion and its works are void except the religion of monotheism. On this reading, al-ḥukm most appropriately means legislative judgment, or a broader judgment that includes creative judgment: legislation belongs to God, and all return to Him rather than to the legislators of other religions.

The commentary records other proposed interpretations: that all creatures are comparatively as though nonexistent because their existence depends on another; that wajh is God’s self or essence; that it is a divine direction identified with bestowed existence; that halāk means death and thus applies only to living things; that wajh means accepted virtuous deeds; that it means God’s established glory and prestige; or that all things are continuously perishing because their existence is renewed at every moment. Some of these readings do not fit the context, some undermine the verse’s proof, and others are far from its meaning.

Finally, al-ḥukm denotes God’s effective judgment and authority by which the order of existence is managed, rather than His judgment on the Day of Resurrection, since the verse mentions judgment before the return that occurs on that Day. “His is the judgment” and “to Him you shall be brought back” each independently prove His exclusive divinity and explain the sincerity owed to Him.
